newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa gets tough on EU trade talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa gets tough on EU trade talks.

text.p: South Africa's Agriculture Ministry threatened on Monday to pull out of trade talks with the European Union and torpedo a proposed free trade area if there was no improvement in the terms offered by the EU.
Officials told a joint meeting of parliament's trade and industry, foreign affairs and agriculture committees that South Africa's negotiating mandate would be ready by October 28.

But they criticised the European offer, which excludes South Africa's major agricultural products from the proposed free trade package, and renewed the country's call for preferential trade terms similar to those offered to other African, Caribbean and Pacific nations in terms of the 1975 Lome Convention.

More than two years after apartheid ended with South Africa's first democratic elections in 1994, President Nelson Mandela's black-led African National Congress government is still trying to cement EU offers of support in a trade treaty.
Members of parliament have criticised the EU for what is seen as a protectionist stance that will deny South Afirca access to European markets for its major products.
Rolf-Joachim Otto, assistant director of national marketing in the department of agriculture, told the committee that the EU mandate for trade talks fell far short of a fair offer.

He said only five percent of South African agricultural exports to the EU were classified less-sensitive or non-sensitive in the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) designed to encourage exports from developing countries.
Most South African exports were listed as sensitive and eligible for minimal preferences or not included in the GSP provisions at all.

"If the EU is not willing to extend any further concessions than those offered in its mandate, the National Department of Agriculture...reserves the right to withdraw from the negotiations and to oppose any free-trade agreement concluded between the EU and South Africa," Otto said.
His statement significantly hardened the South African government's position, which has been criticised both internally and by Commission negotiators as too vague and too soft.
"The EU is discriminating against South Africa," he said.

"Countries with similar levels of development are accorded more favourable treatment on EU markets. The fact remains that South Africa does not present a threat to the EU, either in the agricultural or in the industrial sector," he said.

Department of Trade and Industry official Willem Bosman said South Africa planned further consultations with labour and business and with its neighbours before finalising its negotiating mandate by October 28.
"We have the mandate almost ready," he said, adding that it still had to be approved by the ministers of agriculture, trade and industry, foreign affairs and fiannce.

South Africa's partners in a customs union and in the Southern African Development Community have said in letters to the government and parliament that they want assurances that any deal with the EU would not prejudice them.
